title: Ensemble quant-routing mix probe: latency, cost, and quality tradeoffs
body:
Summary:

This note documents a focused experiment: an end-to-end probe of an "ensemble routing" strategy that routes live-style request mixes between multiple model variants (full-precision FP16 baseline, INT8/GPTQ, AWQ-like 4-bit variant, and an FP8 candidate) using a lightweight classifier and fallback policy. The goal is to measure realistic latency / tail behavior, token-level quality regression, and per-request cost under mixed workload conditions rather than pure synthetic single-stream benchmarks.

Motivation:

We have a growing set of model delivery options (FP16, OPT-GPTQ-int8, AWQ-4bit, experimental FP8). Customers ask how to balance SLOs, cost, and quality in production. Previous quantization benchmarks were microbenchmarks (single prompt template, single kernel selection, steady-state). They show per-token throughput improvements, but they miss: (1) routing overheads, (2) cold-start and prefix-cache effects, (3) quality-sensitive requests where a quantized variant produces unacceptable regressions, and (4) overall unit economics when routing / fallback overheads exist. This experiment attempts to approximate a production routing policy and surface where the runtime needs guardrails (routing thresholds, cache priming, multi-variant fallbacks).

Testbed and constraints:

- Hardware: 8x A100 80GB (multi-tenant cluster slice), isolated test pool.
- Serving runtime: release/2026-03 (kernel selection v2, dynamic batching on).
- Models: M1-FP16 (baseline), M1-GPTQ-int8, M1-AWQ-4bit, M1-FP8-proto (experimental). All variants share same architecture and weights (quantized post-training or q-aware where applicable).
- Ensemble router: decision layer implemented as a tiny tensor classifier that inspects request metadata (estimated output tokens, user tier, prompt fingerprint) and optionally a 1-token "probe" to detect quality-sensitive contexts. Classifier runs in <0.6ms.
- Workload: mixed request trace sampled from production anonymized logs (15k requests): 60% short chat snippets (<=40 tokens), 25% search-snippet generation (<=120 tokens), 10% long-form (>=300 tokens), 5% high-sensitivity eval set (manual prompts flagged by product).
- SLA target: 99th percentile latency per request <= 420ms for interactive tier.

Methodology:

1) Baseline single-variant runs: run the full trace through M1-FP16 to capture baseline latency, tail, and token-level quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding similarity to reference where applicable).
2) Variant microbenchmarks: run trace separately on each quantized variant to measure raw throughput and standalone quality delta.
3) Ensemble routing policies: evaluate three routing policies over the trace:
   - Policy A: Aggressive quant-first: default to AWQ-4bit, fallback to FP16 if similarity/score drops below threshold after full response.
   - Policy B: Conservative tiered: high-sensitivity and long-form -> FP16; remaining -> GPTQ-int8; only cold short-chat -> AWQ-4bit.
   - Policy C: Probe-and-route: send a 1-token probe to AWQ/FP8; if local scoring model predicts likely degradation, route to GPTQ or FP16.
4) Measure: per-request P50/P90/P99 latency, tokens-per-second, per-request cost (compute credits as proxy), quality regressions (embedding similarity and a priority-weighted regression count for the 5% sensitive set), and fallback frequency.

Key results (high level):

- Baseline (FP16): P50=96ms, P90=210ms, P99=410ms; median cost per request = 1.00 unit (normalized). Quality target: reference similarity = 1.0 by definition.

- Single-variant microbenchmarks:
  - AWQ-4bit: raw P50=60ms, P90=150ms, P99=320ms; cost per request = 0.38 units. Overall embedding similarity avg = 0.87 vs FP16. Long-form drift > 0.12 on average (unacceptable for some customers).
  - GPTQ-int8: raw P50=70ms, P90=165ms, P99=340ms; cost = 0.52 units; similarity = 0.93; long-form drift ~0.06.
  - FP8-proto: raw P50=62ms, P90=158ms, P99=335ms; cost = 0.45 units; similarity = 0.90; exhibited higher variance on prompts with deep arithmetic chains (instability in layer norm).

- Ensemble policies (trace-level):
  - Policy A (Aggressive quant-first): overall cost down 54% vs FP16, but 5.8% of requests fell back to FP16 after post-hoc quality check (fallback cost + latency penalty). Effective P99 = 520ms (SLA miss), because fallbacks are amplified for long-form. Quality regressions (priority-weighted) = 7.6%.
  - Policy B (Conservative tiered): cost down 28% vs FP16, P99 = 395ms (meets SLA), fallback frequency = 1.1%, regressions = 1.8% (mostly within acceptable band).
  - Policy C (Probe-and-route): cost down 37% vs FP16, P99 = 410ms (borderline), probe overhead added ~1.2ms average but avoided most post-hoc fallbacks (fallback frequency = 0.9%); regressions = 1.5%. Probe policy reduced wasted computation in long-form fallbacks but introduced a slight increase in P50.

Observations and root causes:

1) Fallbacks are the dominant tail risk. When a quantized path completes then triggers a fallback, the additional latency (rescheduling, KV-cache miss, re-execution) multiplies and shows up in P99. For long-form requests fallback cost can be 2.3x the original request.

2) Cold-prefix and KV cache priming matter. AWQ-style variants suffered more when the prefix wasn't cached; their quantization errors compounded with warm-up kernel path variations, producing larger quality deltas that triggered fallbacks. Ensuring prefix priming on critical routes reduces fallback probability by ~40%.

3) Router classifier errors correlate with request length and domain shift. Classifier precision for "quality-sensitive" prompts was ~82% (precision), meaning misroutes caused unnecessary fallbacks. Probe-and-route improved decision calibration.

4) Kernel selection jitter (different kernels used across variants or batch shapes) introduced small non-deterministic changes that, for long prompts, accumulate and amplify quality differences between variants. This explains why microbenchmarks under steady-state underestimate drift in production mixes.

Practical recommendations for runtime and product:

- Add a routing SLO budget: cap maximum allowed fallback frequency per time window; alert and auto-default to conservative tier when budget exhausted. (Implementation: per-customer fallback counter, circuit-breaker).
- Prefix priming policy: when a request is flagged high-sensitivity or long, ensure KV cache warm-up (replay last 2 tokens or use cached context snapshot) before routing to quant variants. This materially reduced fallback rates in the probe tests.
- Instrument end-to-end fallback latency as a first-class metric in Console: expose cost of fallback per-request so customers can evaluate tradeoffs.
- Improve classifier calibration with a small feedback loop: when a post-response quality-scorer triggers fallback, send that data to retrain router so precision improves over time.
- Kernel determinism toggle: provide a knob in runtime to force deterministic kernel choices for long-form requests to reduce accumulated divergence across variants (costly but beneficial for high-SLA traffic).

Open questions / next experiments:

- Can we implement a lightweight "partial fallback" that re-runs only failed segments for long-form (resume from checkpoint) to reduce full re-execution cost?
- Evaluate quantization-aware KV-cache preservation techniques (store stateless compressed KV in a format compatible across quant variants) to reduce cold-priming divergence.
- Test the ensemble approach under multi-tenant noisy load to measure router stability and false positive rate when GPU contention causes transient kernel choices changes.

Appendix: quick numbers and traces:

- Fallback median extra latency: 180ms (short-chat), 620ms (long-form); fallback median extra cost: 0.42 units/request.
- Probe overhead: 0.8–1.5ms depending on batch shape and kernel path.
- Classifier inference cost: 0.6ms avg per decision (can be amortized for batched frontends).
- Example failure modes: math-heavy prompt where AWQ returns hallucinated numeric sequence; long-context legal prompt where AWQ rephrasing loses clause ordering leading to similarity drop below threshold.

Notes for engineers working on next steps:

- Miguel: prototype the per-customer fallback budget and UI surface in Console.
- Jing: explore KV cache cross-variant compatibility format and prototype a proof-of-concept serializer.
- Omar: run a noisy multi-tenant replay with the probe policy enabled and collect classifier confusion matrix under load to tune thresholds.
- Priya: produce a short customer-facing one-pager summarizing tradeoffs and recommended default: Policy C (probe-and-route) with prefix priming and fallback budget enabled for mid-market customers.

This doc is intentionally rough — notes + numbers from the April run. Will clean and formalize after the noisy-replay and kernel-determinism experiment complete.
